title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper argues AI's next scaling frontier is not bigger models or longer reasoning, but better infrastructure for delivering the right context at decision time.
report.background: AI progress has largely followed two scaling curves: pretraining, where more parameters and data build capability into model weights, and decision-time or test-time scaling, where models search, sample and verify harder before answering. Both assume the missing ingredient is compute. In deployment, however, many failures come from something cheaper and more mundane: the system simply does not have the relevant user state, repository revision, tool trace or sensor reading available when it acts — or has it distorted, stale or badly selected. Retrieval-augmented generation, long-context windows, agent memory and tool-calling frameworks all attack this problem piecemeal, without a shared vocabulary or evaluation method. This position paper proposes treating that work as its own scaling programme with its own budget, and reframes the unit of analysis as the model-plus-infrastructure pair rather than the model alone.
key_points: Three budgets, not one: the paper models a deployed system as a model P(d|c) constrained by a training budget for parameters, a decision-time budget for search and verification, and a context-infrastructure budget for acquiring, storing and delivering state. Only the third determines what is actually available to the model before it decides.

Failures get a taxonomy: the authors separate deployment state from model-visible context and name four failure modes — availability (data was never captured), fidelity (it is noisy or stale), selection (the wrong slice is retrieved) and utilization (the model ignores what it was given). Each needs different fixes.

A five-operation lifecycle: existing mechanisms are organised into a context lifecycle of acquiring, representing, delivering, evaluating and persisting state. This turns scattered engineering tricks into a comparable design space with trade-offs.

Evaluation via budget curves: instead of a single benchmark score, the paper proposes controlled interventions on the context budget and utility-cost curves, measuring how much task performance each increment of context infrastructure buys.

It is an agenda, not a result: the contribution is framing, definitions and a research roadmap centred on grounded reporting, interaction-data infrastructure and safety governance for persistent, adaptive systems — no new model or benchmark numbers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper is a nudge to stop treating context plumbing as glue code and start treating it as a first-class capital expense, which favours vendors of memory, retrieval and observability infrastructure and could shift procurement conversations from tokens to full-cost deployment budgets. For developers, the practical takeaway is diagnostic: before upgrading a model, ask whether the failure was availability, fidelity, selection or utilisation, and instrument accordingly — logging what state existed, what was retrieved and what the model saw. For regular users, the expected benefit is fewer confidently wrong answers caused by missing or stale context, plus clearer accountability: if systems persist state about you, the paper argues governance must cover acquisition and retention, not just model outputs.
report.tools: To explore the ideas hands-on: LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack for probing long-context retrieval; RAGAS for retrieval-augmented generation quality; Letta (formerly MemGPT) and LangGraph checkpointing for persistent agent state; DSPy for optimising retrieval and prompting pipelines; the Model Context Protocol for standardising tool and data delivery; and OpenTelemetry-style tracing (Langfuse, Phoenix) to log what context a model actually received versus what existed.
